bai.moTa: A 1 g rocket: hyperbolas, ceiling clocks faster than floor clocks, and a horizon
bai.yChinh: A uniformly accelerating rocket traces a hyperbola in spacetime that approaches the 45° light ray without ever touching it. The crew’s coordinate grid curves along with the rocket; in that grid a released object “falls,” light bends, a clock at the ceiling runs faster than one at the floor, and a horizon trails behind the rocket. All of this happens in completely flat spacetime.
bai.conSo.1: **0.9687 years**: c/a for a = 1 g; in other words, 1 g ≈ 1.03 light-years per year squared.
bai.conSo.2: **0.775 c** after 1 year on board, **0.968 c** after 2 years.
bai.conSo.3: **2.46 × 10⁻¹⁵**: the fractional difference in clock rate between the top and bottom of a 22.5 m tower (Pound and Rebka 1960).
bai.conSo.4: **19.8 years** on board to reach the galactic center (with braking), while about 26,700 years pass on Earth.
bai.hieuDung: **Spacetime throughout this lesson is completely flat.** A ball “falls,” light “bends,” and higher clocks run faster: all of these are simply consequences of the curved coordinate grid attached to the rocket. True gravity (around a planet) differs in that no single grid can eliminate it everywhere at once; the part that cannot be eliminated is curvature.
bai.nguon: Standard gravitational acceleration 9.80665 m/s² and Julian year 365.25 days. The 22.5 m Harvard tower: Pound and Rebka 1960, Phys. Rev. Lett. 4, 337. Distance to the galactic center 26,700 light-years: GRAVITY 2019–2021 (as in Lesson 2). Alpha Centauri: 4.37 light-years. Every numerical value in this lesson is recomputed in kiem-tra/kiem-rindler.mjs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Explain why a uniformly accelerating rocket has a hyperbolic world line and never reaches the speed of light.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Read the crew’s coordinate grid: lines of “simultaneity” rotate around a pivot point, while the floor and ceiling follow two hyperbolas.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Deduce from the diagram why a ceiling clock runs faster than a floor clock by the factor 1 + ah/c².
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Describe what a Rindler horizon is and why it resembles a black hole horizon.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Calculate travel times for a 1 g voyage using sinh, cosh, and tanh.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
Lesson 7 placed a closed cabin inside a rocket: the crew feels just as heavy as on Earth. Now let us draw that rocket in spacetime. The white grid is an {{khung quán tính|inertial frame}}: horizontal axis $X$ (light-years), vertical axis $cT$ (years). The pink curve is the rocket’s **floor**.

“Uniform acceleration at 1 g” means that the crew, using an onboard accelerometer, **always** measures an acceleration of 9.81 m/s². That is {{gia tốc riêng|proper acceleration}}. Seen from the inertial frame, the rocket’s speed keeps increasing, but more and more slowly as it nears $c$, because velocity addition as in Lesson 6 never exceeds $c$. The result is a **hyperbola**:

$$ X^2 - c^2T^2 = \left(\frac{c^2}{a}\right)^2 $$

At $T = 0$ the rocket is momentarily at rest at $X = c^2/a$. Afterward it approaches the 45° light ray (yellow line) without ever touching it. This is {{chuyển động hyperbol|hyperbolic motion}}.

> [Con số] For $a$ = 1 g: $c/a = 0{,}9687$ years and $c^2/a = 0{,}9687$ light-years. In other words, 1 g $\approx 1{,}03$ light-years per year squared. That is why the numbers in this lesson stay neatly around 1.

> [Thử ngay] Labels along the floor mark the speed after every half-year on the rocket’s clock: after 1 year it is already 0.77 c, and after 2 years 0.97 c. Drag the small rocket (the pink dot at its base) along the world line to read its speed at each moment.
> [[Front view|thang]] [[Angled view|cheo]]

> [Lưu ý] The small rocket in the diagram lies along the crew’s line of “simultaneity,” with its base on the floor and its exhaust pointing backward. The engine’s hum stays **unchanged** throughout the flight: what the crew feels is proper acceleration, and it is always 1 g, even though the rocket speeds up as seen from the inertial frame.

+++ Go deeper: why it is a hyperbola
Let $\tau$ be the crew’s proper time and $\varphi$ the rapidity (Lesson 6), with $v/c = \tanh\varphi$. Over a brief interval $\dd\tau$, the rocket defines an instantaneous inertial frame and gains velocity $a\,\dd\tau$ **in that frame**. Because rapidities add directly, $\dd\varphi = a\,\dd\tau/c$, so $\varphi = a\tau/c$.

The four-velocity is $u = c\,(\cosh\varphi,\ \sinh\varphi)$. Integrating with respect to $\tau$ gives

$$ cT = \frac{c^2}{a}\sinh\frac{a\tau}{c}, \qquad X = \frac{c^2}{a}\cosh\frac{a\tau}{c} $$

Using $\cosh^2 - \sinh^2 = 1$ yields the hyperbola equation above. Seen from the inertial frame, the velocity is $v = c\tanh(a\tau/c)$, which is always less than $c$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.de: Drag the rocket along its world line until its speed reaches **0.9 c** relative to the inertial frame (within 0.01 c).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.goiY: $v = c\tanh(a\tau/c)$. Both the data panel and the label beside the rocket display $v$. A speed of 0.9 c is reached after about 1.4 years on board, just when Earth’s clock reads 2 years.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Now add the rocket’s **ceiling** (blue), at height $h$ = 0.4 light-years above the floor. For the rocket to stay rigid (floor and ceiling always separated by $h$ according to the crew’s rulers), the ceiling must trace a **different** hyperbola sharing the same center:

$$ X^2 - c^2T^2 = \left(\frac{c^2}{a} + h\right)^2 $$

The faint green rays through the origin are the crew’s lines of “simultaneity,” spaced every 0.25 years on the floor clock. Each ray is the $x'$ axis of the rocket’s instantaneous inertial frame (Lesson 6): later on, the rocket moves faster, so the ray tilts further. All the rays **rotate around the same pivot point** at the origin. The bright green sheet is the crew’s “now,” rotating along with them.

Together, the hyperbolas and rays form the grid of {{tọa độ Rindler|Rindler coordinates}} $(\rho,\ \eta)$: $\rho$ is the “height” (constant along each hyperbola), and $\eta$ is the ray’s “angle.”

> [Lưu ý] A rocket 0.4 light-years tall is absurd; that height is chosen only to make the geometry visible. For a real rocket about 30 m tall, the effect is smaller by roughly a hundred trillion times, yet it is real and measurable (step 4).

> [Thử ngay] Switch to the rocket frame: the curved grid straightens into rectangles, the floor and ceiling stand vertical, and the lines of “simultaneity” lie horizontal.
> [[Rocket frame|tl]] [[Inertial frame|qt]]

To keep a constant separation, **the floor must accelerate harder than the ceiling**: the proper acceleration at height $\rho$ is $c^2/\rho$. When the floor feels 1 g, the ceiling feels only $\rho_0/(\rho_0 + h) \approx 0{,}71$ g. Nothing about this is peculiar to one design: relativity does not allow any rigid body to accelerate at the same rate everywhere.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: Dropping a ball: gravity from a curved grid
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
At $\eta = 0$ (when the rocket is momentarily at rest), the crew releases a ball from the ceiling. From that moment nothing pushes on the ball, so in the inertial frame it **stays at rest forever**: its world line is the vertical line $X = \rho_0 + h$ (white). Meanwhile the rocket’s floor keeps accelerating, rushing up to meet the ball at

$$ cT = \sqrt{(\rho_0 + h)^2 - \rho_0^2} \approx 0{,}967 \text{ years} $$

in the inertial frame, or $0{,}85$ years on the floor clock.

> [Thử ngay] Switch to the rocket frame: the floor stands still while the ball **curves toward the floor**, speeding up as it goes. To the crew, the ball falls just as on Earth.
> [[Rocket frame|tl]] [[Inertial frame|qt]] [[Front view|thang]]

It is the very same world line, straight in one grid and curved in the other. The “force” pulling the ball downward comes from nowhere: it is simply a consequence of **choosing the curved coordinate grid** attached to the rocket. That is Einstein’s insight from Lesson 7 drawn in spacetime: the gravity inside the cabin can be transformed away by changing grids.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “The ball’s world line bends when we change frames.” No. A world line is a set of events and never changes. Only the coordinates assigned to those events change, so the drawn curve changes accordingly.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The floor clock emits a flash of light every 0.25 years (yellow lines rising at 45°). Pink dots mark ticks of the floor clock. Blue dots mark ticks of the ceiling clock, also every 0.25 years **on the ceiling clock itself**. Yellow dots mark when each flash reaches the ceiling.

A light ray climbing from floor to ceiling spans the same “angle” $\Delta\eta$ whenever it is emitted, so the ceiling receives the flashes **equally spaced** in $\eta$, just as the floor sent them. Yet proper time along the hyperbola at height $\rho$ is $\tau = \rho\,\eta/c$: over the same $\Delta\eta$, the ceiling clock counts more time than the floor clock by the exact ratio

$$ \frac{\Delta\tau_{\text{ceiling}}}{\Delta\tau_{\text{floor}}} = \frac{\rho_0 + h}{\rho_0} = 1 + \frac{ah}{c^2} \approx 1{,}413 $$

In the diagram, 0.25 years on the floor corresponds to 0.353 years on the ceiling. Higher clocks run faster; upward-traveling light arrives spaced farther apart in local time, and therefore redder.

> [Thử ngay] Rocket frame: the light rays **curve**, and the blue dots along the ceiling are packed more closely than the pink dots along the floor. Drag the **third clock** (purple dot on the horizontal axis) higher or lower: its purple dots crowd together or spread out in exact proportion to $\rho/\rho_0$.
> [[Rocket frame|tl]] [[Inertial frame|qt]]

> [Lưu ý] About the sound: each clock ticks once every 0.25 years of its own time (low pitch for the floor, higher for the ceiling, highest for the third clock). You can hear the ceiling ticking more rapidly than the floor. In the animation, 1 year on the floor clock lasts about 2.4 seconds.

> [Lịch sử] Pound and Rebka (1960) sent gamma rays up and down a 22.5 m tower at Harvard University. By the equivalence principle, standing on the ground is like riding in a 1 g rocket, so the frequency must shift by $gh/c^2 = 9{,}81 \times 22{,}5/(2{,}998 \times 10^8)^2 \approx 2{,}46 \times 10^{-15}$. Their measurements matched this prediction. Lesson 9 continues with clocks in real gravity.

+++ Go deeper: why Δη is constant, and why τ = ρη
Set $c = 1$ and use light-cone coordinates $u = T - X$, $v = T + X$. Along the hyperbola at height $\rho$: $X = \rho\cosh\eta$ and $T = \rho\sinh\eta$, so $u = -\rho e^{-\eta}$ and $v = \rho e^{\eta}$.

1. A light ray traveling toward $+X$ keeps $u$ constant.
2. Emitted from the floor at $\eta_1$, it has $u = -\rho_0 e^{-\eta_1}$. It reaches the ceiling when $-\rho_1 e^{-\eta_2} = -\rho_0 e^{-\eta_1}$, giving $\eta_2 = \eta_1 + \ln(\rho_1/\rho_0)$.
3. Every ray therefore takes the same $\Delta\eta = \ln(\rho_1/\rho_0)$: two flashes emitted $\delta\eta$ apart arrive $\delta\eta$ apart.
4. Proper time along a hyperbola satisfies $\dd\tau^2 = \dd T^2 - \dd X^2 = \rho^2(\cosh^2\eta - \sinh^2\eta)\,\dd\eta^2 = \rho^2\dd\eta^2$, so $\tau = \rho\,\eta$.
5. Floor: $\delta\tau_0 = \rho_0\,\delta\eta$. Ceiling: $\delta\tau_1 = \rho_1\,\delta\eta$. Their ratio is $\rho_1/\rho_0 = 1 + h/\rho_0 = 1 + ah/c^2$ with $\rho_0 = c^2/a$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the third clock to the height where it runs **twice as fast** as the floor clock (within 0.05).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: The rate ratio is $\rho/\rho_0$ with $\rho_0 = 0{,}97$ light-years. Twice as fast means twice as far from the pivot point as the floor, where the proper acceleration drops to 0.5 g.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
The orange-red glass sheet tilted at 45° is the surface $cT = X$. Even traveling at the speed of light, no signal emitted **beyond** this surface (above it in the diagram) can ever catch up with the rocket, as long as the rocket keeps accelerating. Nothing there can ever be seen by the crew. This surface is the {{chân trời Rindler|Rindler horizon}}.

To watch this happen, the crew drops a **beacon** through a floor hatch at $\eta = 0$. The beacon remains at rest in the inertial frame (orange line) and flashes toward the rocket every 0.1 years on its own clock.

- The flash emitted at 0.5 years reaches the floor at 0.70 years (floor clock); the flash emitted at 0.9 years arrives at 2.56 years.
- The beacon crosses the horizon at 0.9687 years. Flashes emitted afterward (faint red lines) travel parallel to the horizon forever and never arrive.

> [Thử ngay] Rocket frame: the beacon falls toward the horizon (crowding toward $\rho = 0$), **slowing down** without ever crossing it; its flashes arrive farther and farther apart—growing redder—and fade out. The crew never sees the beacon cross the horizon, even though for the beacon itself nothing special happens at the crossing.
> [[Rocket frame|tl]] [[Inertial frame|qt]]

> [Thử ngay] In the inertial frame, drag the **emission event** (yellow dot on the orange line) up and down: the yellow ray is your signal. If the rocket left Earth at $T = 0$, the orange line is Earth itself: any message sent from home after 0.97 years will never reach the crew.

> [Lưu ý] About the sound: each beacon flash reaching the floor plays a musical note. Its frequency is 660 Hz multiplied by the ratio of received to emitted rate, $1 - T_e/\rho_0$: the notes **grow sparser and deeper**, mirroring the redshift of the light. This is an audible mapping, not the actual frequency of the light.

This is the exact counterpart of an object falling into a black hole as seen from afar (Lesson 16): slowing, reddening, and fading at the horizon. Here the horizon is neither a physical object nor a wall; it is created by the observer’s motion. If the rocket stops accelerating, the horizon disappears.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: Drag the emission event up along the orange line to send a signal that the rocket **never receives**.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: The signal travels to the right at 45°. It catches up with the rocket only when emitted below the horizon cT = X. The orange line crosses the horizon at 0.97 years.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: The equivalence principle, and its limits
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
To sum up: standing on the ground feels just like riding in a 1 g rocket. In both settings, dropped objects fall, light bends, and higher clocks run faster. That is the {{nguyên lý tương đương|equivalence principle}} from Lesson 7, now complete with its spacetime picture.

Notice, however, that **spacetime throughout this lesson remains flat**. The white inertial grid still extends everywhere, and straight lines are still straight. Every “gravitational” effect comes solely from the curvature of the rocket’s coordinate grid.

> [Thử ngay] Switch back and forth between the two grids. It is the same geometry with two coordinate systems.
> [[Rocket frame|tl]] [[Inertial frame|qt]] [[Front view|thang]] [[Angled view|cheo]]

Real gravity around a planet differs in one decisive way: **no single inertial grid can eliminate it everywhere at once**.

- Inside the rocket, all dropped objects fall along parallel paths in the same direction. Switching to an inertial frame removes the falling everywhere.
- Around Earth, a ball in Hanoi falls toward Earth’s center and a ball in Buenos Aires also falls toward Earth’s center—nearly opposite directions. A freely falling frame that cancels gravity in Hanoi cannot cancel it in Buenos Aires.

What cannot be canceled away is spacetime {{độ cong|curvature}}, revealed by {{lực thủy triều|tidal forces}}. Lesson 10 and Lesson 12 develop this idea.

> [Tóm lại] The equivalence principle holds only **within a sufficiently small region**. Locally, gravity can be transformed away; on a global scale it cannot, and that irreducible part is true gravity.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: A 1 g voyage: reaching the galactic center in a human lifetime
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Now let us use the hyperbola to plan an interstellar voyage. A spacecraft accelerates continuously at 1 g, and $\tau$ is the number of years elapsed **on board**:

$$ cT = \frac{c^2}{a}\sinh\frac{a\tau}{c}, \qquad v = c\tanh\frac{a\tau}{c} $$

$$ d = \frac{c^2}{a}\left(\cosh\frac{a\tau}{c} - 1\right) $$

| Ship time $\tau$ | Earth time $T$ | Distance $d$ | Speed $v$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 yr | 1.19 yr | 0.56 light-years | 0.775 c |
| 2 yr | 3.76 yr | 2.91 light-years | 0.968 c |
| 3 yr | 10.7 yr | 9.77 light-years | 0.9959 c |
| 5 yr | 84.5 yr | 83.5 light-years | 0.99993 c |
| 10 yr | 14,736 yr | 14,735 light-years | nearly c |

After a few years, $\sinh$ and $\cosh$ grow exponentially: each additional year on board multiplies the distance covered by nearly 2.8.

> [Con số] **To the galactic center**, 26,700 light-years away, accelerating for the first half and braking for the second half so as to arrive at rest: only about **19.8 years** pass on board, while about **26,700 years** pass on Earth. Without braking (a flyby), the trip takes just 10.6 years on board.

> [Thử ngay] Drag **Years on board**, or click:
> [[To the galactic center|ngan]] [[To Alpha Centauri|alpha]] [[Accelerate continuously for 5 years|nam5]]

> [Lưu ý] The diagram scales to fit the view: horizontal and vertical axes share the same scale (light still travels at 45°), and that scale adjusts with the trip. Fuel is ignored: no real rocket could carry enough energy for such a journey.

The crew’s proper time is the “length” of the pink curve: just 19.8 years, while roughly 26,700 years pass on Earth. A ship coasting at constant velocity between the very same departure and arrival events would record a longer proper time than the pink curve, just as in Lesson 6: between two events, the straight world line has the longest proper time.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: A hyperbola asymptotic to the 45° light ray. For 1 g, c²/a = 0.9687 light-years.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: $\tau$: proper time of the crew. Rapidity grows uniformly: $\varphi = a\tau/c$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: $\rho$: height (constant on each hyperbola); $\eta$: angle of the line of “simultaneity.” Proper acceleration at height $\rho$ is $c^2/\rho$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: On Earth: $gh/c^2$, about $1{,}1 \times 10^{-16}$ per meter of height.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: A rocket accelerates uniformly at 1 g forever. Seen from Earth, what happens to its speed?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: It increases by 9.8 m/s every second and exceeds c after about a year
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: It keeps increasing, approaching c ever more closely without ever reaching it
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.3: It rises to c and then stays constant
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.4: It decreases over time because its mass grows
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: $v = c\tanh(a\tau/c)$ is always less than $c$. The crew still feels a steady 1 g, but as seen from Earth each velocity increment combines via the velocity-addition formula from Lesson 6, so the speed never exceeds $c$. The first choice uses Newtonian addition.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Inside an accelerating rocket, compare a clock on the ceiling with a clock on the floor: which one runs faster, and according to whom?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.1: The floor clock runs faster, because the floor accelerates harder
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.2: The ceiling clock runs faster, and everyone inside the rocket agrees
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.3: Both clocks run at the same rate because they share the same rocket
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.4: It depends on whether the observer stands on the ceiling or on the floor
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: The ceiling receives flashes from the floor less frequently, while the floor receives flashes from the ceiling more frequently: both agree that the ceiling clock runs faster by the factor $1 + ah/c^2$. Unlike time dilation between uniformly moving observers (which is symmetric), the two clocks here are at rest relative to each other, so their rates can be compared unambiguously.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: A ball is released from the ceiling of an accelerating rocket. What does the ball do in an inertial frame?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.1: It accelerates downward toward the floor at 1 g
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: It stays at rest (or moves at constant velocity); the floor rushes up to meet it
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: Once released, nothing pushes on the ball, so its world line is straight. “Falling” appears only when the motion is described in the rocket’s coordinate grid.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Why does the crew never see the dropped beacon cross the horizon?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: Because the beacon is destroyed before reaching the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: Because light emitted at or beyond the horizon can never catch up with the accelerating rocket
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.3: Because the horizon is a physical wall
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.4: Because the beacon comes to a halt at the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: On its own clock, the beacon crosses the horizon uneventfully after about a year (0.97 years). Signals emitted from the horizon onward, however, travel parallel to the horizon and never reach the rocket. Signals emitted just before the crossing arrive ever later and farther apart, so the crew sees the beacon slow down and redden.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: A ship accelerates continuously at 1 g for 3 years of ship time (without braking). How far is it from Earth, and how much time has passed on Earth?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: $a\tau/c = 3/0{,}9687 \approx 3{,}10$. Then $cT = 0{,}9687 \sinh 3{,}10 \approx 10{,}7$ years and $d = 0{,}9687(\cosh 3{,}10 - 1) \approx 9{,}77$ light-years. The last choice corresponds to 5 years.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: The equivalence principle says that standing on the ground feels like riding in a 1 g rocket. Is Earth’s gravity therefore nothing more than “choosing a curved coordinate grid,” as inside the rocket?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Only within a small region. Inside the rocket, all dropped objects fall along parallel paths, so a single inertial frame eliminates “gravity” everywhere because spacetime is flat. Around Earth, objects on opposite sides fall toward the center in opposite directions, and objects at different altitudes fall with different accelerations. No inertial grid can eliminate gravity everywhere at once. What remains—tidal forces—is genuine spacetime curvature.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: C. W. Misner, K. S. Thorne, and J. A. Wheeler, *Gravitation* (1973), chapter 6: accelerated observers and coordinates of a uniformly accelerated observer.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: B. Schutz, *A First Course in General Relativity* (2nd ed., 2009), chapter 5: why gravity cannot be a force in flat spacetime; the Pound–Rebka tower inside a rocket.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapters 5 and 6: uniform acceleration, the equivalence principle, and gravitational redshift.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: Pound and Rebka 1960, Phys. Rev. Lett. 4, 337: measurement of gravitational redshift on a 22.5 m tower.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: The acceleration measured by an onboard accelerometer. An object in free fall has proper acceleration 0; a person standing on the ground has an upward proper acceleration of 1 g.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: Motion with constant proper acceleration. Its world line is the hyperbola $X^2 - c^2T^2 = (c^2/a)^2$, asymptotic to a light ray.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: Coordinates $(\rho,\ \eta)$ adapted to a family of uniformly accelerating observers: $X = \rho\cosh\eta$, $cT = \rho\sinh\eta$. Spacetime remains flat; only the coordinate grid is curved.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The surface cT = X: signals emitted beyond it never reach the uniformly accelerating observer. Created by the observer’s motion, it vanishes if acceleration stops.
